Issued at 240 PM CDT Tue Sep 8 2026

Rest of Today - Tonight:

As of 230 PM this afternoon, regional satellite imagery shows 
much of the Northland under cloud cover ahead of a cold front 
now moving into portions of central to north-central Minnesota, 
with rapid clearing behind it. This extensive cloud cover has 
kept much of the area capped to thunderstorm development so far 
today aside from a few scattered showers/non-severe storms that 
have been moving through north-central Minnesota. CAMs continue 
to be fairly reserved regarding additional scattered shower and
thunderstorm development along the cold front later this 
afternoon and evening as it propagates east across the area as 
the cloud cover makes it difficult to break through low-level 
capping in addition to drier air moving in aloft. If the capping
inversion were to break, then there is potential for a few 
strong storms to develop mainly in east-central Minnesota to 
northwest Wisconsin in the 4 PM - 9 PM timeframe and access 
800-1500 J/kg of MLCAPE amid 40-50 kt of a fairly unidirectional
effective shear profile. Storm intensity and coverage would 
then wane around and after sunset in northwest Wisconsin. The 
hazards with any strong storms would be hail up to penny size, 
wind gusts to 40 mph, and locally heavy downpours.

Lingering moisture in the lowest-levels of the atmosphere behind
the cold front tonight in northwest Wisconsin should lead to
patchy fog as winds become light. 

Wednesday - Thursday: 

While the cold front will be east of the Northland on Wednesday
and surface high pressure will be slowly building in for mid-
week, cyclonic flow and some lingering low-level moisture could
lead to some sprinkles or very light rain showers (10-20%
chance) north of the Iron Range and into the Arrowhead daytime
Wednesday. Little to no accumulations expected. Wednesday will
also see very strong daytime west-northwest winds with gusts of
25-40 mph, being strongest in the Arrowhead, particularly in the
higher terrain of the North Shore. Probabilities for >45 mph
wind gusts continue to decrease, so don't anticipate any need
for a Wind Advisory. Expect a near-seasonal day for high
temperatures on Wednesday, ranging from the upper 60s to mid 
70s. Low temperatures become cooler Wednesday night into the
40s, though the typical cold spots could touch the upper 30s
under clear skies and light winds.

Less windy southwest winds and a dry forecast are in store for 
Thursday under clear to mostly clear skies and high temperatures
ranging from around 70 degrees into the upper 70s.

Friday - This Weekend:

We see a couple rounds of precipitation chances return for
Friday into this weekend. The first round would be with a
surface low ejecting out of the northern Plains daytime Friday
and through northern Minnesota Friday PM into early Saturday
morning. Strong warm/moist advection with this system in
combination with strong synoptic forcing for ascent driven by a
strong mid/upper-level shortwave trough and jet could set the 
stage for isolated to scattered strong to severe storms Friday 
afternoon and evening when the best instability/strong shear 
combination would overlap. Still some question as to how far 
north the warm-sector of this low pressure system would make it 
into the Northland depending on the forecast ensemble low 
tracks. As of now, the portion of the Northland with the best 
potential for strong to severe storms would be along/south of 
US-2 in northeast Minnesota into far northwest Wisconsin. Storm 
intensities should wane towards Friday night, with 
showers/remnant non-severe storms ending west to east into early
Saturday morning.

Additional showers and perhaps a few general storms are 
possible (10-30% chance) on Sunday with weak troughing moving 
though largely zonal flow aloft, but instability will be limited
at best, so likely to be mainly just showers.

We also see the shift to a cooler pattern starting this weekend
with high temperatures in the low 60s to low 70s on Saturday and
60s on Sunday. Lows Saturday and Sunday nights could even touch
the upper 30s to mid 40s, though the typical cold spots could
see mid-30s even! For now, the potential for areas of frost
remains less than 20%.

Early Next Week:

The cool pattern persists into early next week with highs in the
60s and possibly even some upper 50s on Monday, with nightly
lows in the upper 30s to 40s. Global ensemble members and
deterministic models show fairly good agreement on a more
robust, Colorado low-type system developing in the lee of the
Rockies as a deeper mid/upper-level trough moves across the High
Plains into Upper Midwest Sunday night through Monday night.
This would bring a good shot at more widespread rain and 
appreciable rainfall amounts should the forecast system track 
hold over the next several days.
